report:
### Conclusion
High-quality clinical evidence indicates that **ivermectin does not lower the risk of death** or improve clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19. 

### Evidence Summary
* **Large Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs):** Well-designed, large-scale trials have consistently demonstrated that ivermectin lacks efficacy against COVID-19. For example, the TOGETHER platform trial evaluated symptomatic outpatients and found that early treatment with ivermectin did not reduce hospital admissions or prevent disease progression (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869). Likewise, the ACTIV-6 trial concluded that ivermectin was ineffective as a COVID-19 treatment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivermectin_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic).
* **Limitations of Early Studies:** Early reports that suggested a mortality benefit often suffered from small sample sizes, high risk of bias, or methodological flaws. Some early influential trials claiming significant treatment effects were subsequently withdrawn due to data integrity concerns (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9006771/).
* **Regulatory and Health Guidance:** Health authorities and regulatory agencies, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), confirm that available clinical data do not demonstrate that ivermectin is effective for treating or preventing COVID-19 in humans (https://www.drugs.com/ivermectin.html).

Overall, rigorous evidence from large RCTs does not support using ivermectin to reduce mortality in COVID-19 patients.
